batchName: Late Republic: Cicero, Catiline and the Triumvirate (63-53 BCE) - Medium Batch 2
chapterName: Late Republic: Cicero, Catiline and the Triumvirate (63-53 BCE)

questions.question: How were the Parthian mounted archers at Carrhae kept supplied with arrows?
options: By river boats on the Euphrates
questions.explanation: A camel train kept the archers resupplied as they rained arrows on the Roman square. The Parthian force numbered about 10,000 cavalry.
questions.sourceQuote: Mounted archers rained arrows on the Roman square, resupplied by a train of camels.

questions.question: By how much did Caesar cut the tax companies' debt to please Crassus?
questions.explanation: Caesar reduced the tax companies' debt by a third. In the same year he also approved Pompey's eastern settlement.
questions.sourceQuote: Caesar then cut the tax companies' debt by a third for Crassus and approved Pompey's eastern settlement.

questions.question: What happened to Caesar's fellow consul when he tried to block the vote on the land law?
options: He was assassinated in the Forum
A mob threw him from the platform and broke his fasces
Caesar had him dragged off to jail
Tribunes stripped him of his office
Pompey's veterans forced him into exile
questions.explanation: A mob hurled him from the speakers' platform and broke his fasces, the symbol of consular authority. Afterwards he shut himself at home, declaring bad omens.
questions.sourceQuote: When the fellow consul tried to block the vote, a mob threw him from the speakers' platform and broke his fasces, the bundle of rods around an axe carried before a consul as a symbol of his authority.

questions.question: What role did Caesar play in forming the alliance with Pompey and Crassus?
questions.explanation: Pompey and Crassus were rivals who could cooperate only through an intermediary, and Caesar filled that role. The pact was struck sometime between July 60 and January 59 BC.
questions.sourceQuote: Pompey and Crassus were personal rivals who could only cooperate through a go-between, and Caesar was that man.

questions.question: What did Caesar propose for the arrested conspirators on 5 December 63 BC?
options: Life imprisonment or custody until trial
questions.explanation: Caesar's milder plan of life imprisonment or custody until trial won many over, though it was also illegal. The senior senators had all called for death.
questions.sourceQuote: Then Caesar, a rising politician due to take high office the next year, proposed life imprisonment or custody until trial.

questions.question: How did the Roman politician who wrote a short history of the plot about twenty years later portray Catiline?
options: As a villain symbolising the republic's moral decay
As a wronged reformer championing the poor
As a heroic general betrayed by the Senate
As a minor figure in Cicero's career
As a puppet manipulated by Crassus
questions.explanation: This historian, who had been abroad in 63 BC, leaned heavily on Cicero. He made Catiline a villain bent on destroying Rome from the start.
questions.sourceQuote: He leaned heavily on Cicero and portrayed Catiline as a villain bent on destroying Rome from the start, a symbol of the moral decay he believed was ruining the republic.

questions.question: Historians who doubt the trio's power note that the allies won big only when?
options: Only when fully united, as in 59 and 55 BC
Only when Caesar was in Rome
questions.explanation: Sceptics note that the allies often lost elections and quarrelled constantly. Others see their pact as the moment the free republic died.
questions.sourceQuote: Others point out that the allies often lost elections, quarrelled constantly, and won big only when fully united, as in 59 and 55 BC.

questions.question: What happened as Crassus left Rome for Syria in November 55 BC?
options: Pompey escorted him to the coast
A tribune solemnly cursed him at the city gate
The Senate voted him a triumph in advance
questions.explanation: A tribune cursed Crassus at the city gate on 14 November 55 BC. The allies' naked use of force that year had confirmed critics' warnings of tyranny.
questions.sourceQuote: When Crassus left for Syria on 14 November 55 BC, a tribune solemnly cursed him at the city gate.

questions.question: Whose offer of a safer route into Parthian territory did Crassus twice refuse?
questions.explanation: Crassus twice turned down the Armenian king's offer of a route through Armenia. Wintering in Syria also cost him the advantage of surprise.
questions.sourceQuote: He twice refused the Armenian king's offer of a safer route through Armenia, and after early successes spent the winter in Syria, losing the advantage of surprise.

questions.question: What did the Senate's so-called final decree (senatus consultum ultimum) do?
options: Granted the consuls legal immunity for any action
Appointed a dictator for six months
Urged the consuls to do whatever it took to protect the state
Ordered the immediate arrest of Catiline
questions.explanation: The final decree urged the consuls to take whatever action was needed to protect the state. It did not, however, give Cicero legal immunity.
questions.sourceQuote: The Senate (*senatus*) declared an emergency and passed its so-called final decree (*senatus consultum ultimum*), urging the consuls to do whatever it took to protect the state.
